clinical_record:
A 33-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with a 3-month history of progressively worsening occipital headache, exacerbated by Valsalva maneuvers. On neurologic examination, he had bilateral past-pointing and an intention tremor. Brain MRI revealed a 6.9 × 5.5 × 6.1 cm lobulated mass centered at the left cerebellopontine angle, extending craniocaudally from the left ambient cistern to the premedullary space. The lesion involved and expanded Meckel’s cave, with a small extension into the left infratemporal fossa via the foramen ovale. It contained multiloculated T1-hypointense, T2-FLAIR–partially suppressible nonenhancing cystic areas with interspersed enhancing septa, as well as T1/T2-isointense enhancing solid components. Susceptibility-weighted imaging demonstrated curvilinear signal loss with corresponding T1 hyperintensity consistent with hemorrhagic foci, and diffusion-weighted imaging showed no diffusion restriction. There was compression of the left cerebellum and brainstem, dilation of the third, fourth, and lateral ventricles, anterior displacement of the cavernous sinus, and encasement with mild narrowing of the left petrous internal carotid artery; the masticator muscles were preserved. Noncontrast CT of the head showed smooth remodeling and erosion of the left petrous apex, clivus, carotid canal, and foramen ovale, along with two punctate calcifications; the internal auditory canals and inner ear structures were unremarkable.

clinical_record:
An 18-year-old man presented with 6 months of fluctuating lower-limb weakness. He awoke one morning unable to move his legs but recovered movement over 30 minutes, with residual unsteadiness. He remained asymptomatic for 4 months, then developed ascending spastic weakness of the lower limbs over 3 months until he was unable to stand, accompanied by urinary retention requiring a Foley catheter and one month of constipation. He denied trauma, fever, steroid or other drug intake, and infections.

On examination he was non-obese (65 kg, 167 cm; BMI 23.3 kg/m2) with no signs of Cushing syndrome or endocrinopathy. Neurologic examination showed increased tone and preserved bulk in the lower limbs, Medical Research Council grade 3/5 at hips and knees and 0/5 at ankles and toes, brisk knee and ankle jerks, bilateral extensor plantar responses, and graded sensory loss below the D10 level. The spine was neither deformed nor tender. Routine hematological and biochemical tests and cerebrospinal fluid analysis were normal. Plain radiographs of the spine were unremarkable.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracic spine demonstrated a posterior epidural mass from D5 to D7, with a maximum thickness of 10 mm that was homogeneously hyperintense on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted sequences, suggestive of fat.

A 65-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of a slowly progressive orbital mass causing left exophthalmia, left hemifacial pain, and progressive visual impairment culminating in total vision loss.  
Her medical history included 8 years of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, stage IIB cervical adenocarcinoma treated 3 years earlier with concurrent radiotherapy and weekly cisplatin, and well-controlled hypertension, dyslipidemia, and hypothyroidism.  
On examination, she had left exophthalmia with vision impairment and complete restriction of ocular motility. Anterior rhinoscopy, oral cavity, and neck examinations were unremarkable; nasofibrolaryngoscopy revealed a discrete medial bulging of the left nasal fossa lateral wall and a leftward septal deviation.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbital region showed a soft-tissue density lesion occupying the left maxillary sinus with extension into the orbit, ethmoidal and sphenoid sinuses, and bone discontinuity of the maxillary, septal, sphenoid, ethmoidal walls, and pterygopalatine fossa. MRI demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing mass in the left maxillary sinus, nasal cavity, ethmoidal sinuses, and intraorbital region, with bone disruption of the lateral and inferior orbital walls, extension through the inferior orbital fissure, invasion of the left cavernous sinus, diffusion restriction around the ophthalmic nerve, and anterior displacement of the extraocular muscles and vessels; these findings were considered highly suggestive of malignant neoplasm.  
Laboratory studies on admission showed HbA1c 8.8%, CRP 15.5 mg/L, ESR 120 mm/h, negative Cryptococcus antigen, nonreactive FTA-ABS, HIV, and hepatitis panels except positive anti-HBc, and CSF analysis with protein 58 mg/dL, glucose 66 mg/dL, WBC 5/mm3, IgG 11.3 mg/dL, negative cytology and cultures, and ADA 1.8 U/L.  
An endoscopic endonasal biopsy of the left maxillary sinus revealed on frozen section a probable low-grade lymphoproliferative lesion, but paraffin-fixed sections showed nonspecific chronic fibrosing inflammation without evidence of neoplasia, granulomas, or fungi.

clinical_record:
A 78-year-old man presented with a 4-week history of productive cough, occasional hemoptysis, and epistaxis. His medical history included hypertension and treated tuberculosis; he was an ex–cigarette smoker. Physical examination was unremarkable. A chest radiograph showed a spiculated 3.5 cm mass in the right lower zone. CT of the thorax demonstrated a 5 cm cavitating mass in the right lower lobe with bilateral small cavitating nodules. Laboratory tests revealed a cytoplasmic ANCA titre of 1 / 20 and a PR3 level of 14.6 IU ml−1. CT-guided biopsy of the right lower lobe mass showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation without evidence of malignancy. The patient was started on subcutaneous methotrexate, and after 3 months a chest radiograph showed reduction of the nodule to 2 cm. He then developed renal impairment attributed to disease progression and/or methotrexate toxicity, and treatment was switched to high-dose intravenous cyclophosphamide with a tapering dose of oral prednisolone. After 3 months of cyclophosphamide, he developed a new cough and chest radiography showed enlargement of the right lower lobe nodule to 4 cm; CT confirmed an increase to a 5 cm cavitating mass at the same location.

He denied anorexia, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, weight loss, night sweats, diarrhea, or constipation. On examination, he was afebrile; heart rate was 86 bpm, and blood pressure was 130/95 mm Hg. Abdominal examination showed voluntary guarding in the right lower quadrant and minimal tenderness elsewhere. Laboratory tests revealed a white-cell count of 15,600/mL, hemoglobin of 14.2 g/dL, and platelet count of 126,000/mL. Plain abdominal X-rays demonstrated several air–fluid levels without free air under the diaphragm. Ultrasound assessment was interpreted as compatible with plastron appendicitis. Computed tomography of the abdomen revealed a linear lesion within the intestinal lumen in the right lower quadrant, causing partial luminal obliteration and edema on the anterolateral aspect of the cecum.

A 53-year-old Hispanic man with no prior comorbidities presented with a two-week history of recurrent cough, nonmassive hemoptysis, and central chest pain. One month earlier, he had mild COVID-19 not requiring hospitalization. He also reported fatigue, myalgias, and anorexia but denied fever, dyspnea, or gastrointestinal symptoms.

On examination, he was tachycardic but in no acute distress; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (25.56×10^3/μL), blood urea nitrogen 107 mg/dL, creatinine 5.8 mg/dL (baseline unknown), mild transaminitis, hyponatremia, and hypoalbuminemia. Urinalysis and urine indices were ordered.

A chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral scattered infiltrates with a denser consolidation in the right upper lobe. Noncontrast chest CT revealed multiple peripheral patchy consolidations in both lungs, some cavitating. These findings were interpreted as multifocal pneumonia.

He received intravenous azithromycin and ceftriaxone, intravenous bicarbonate, and emergent hemodialysis for acute kidney injury. Blood, sputum, and urine cultures were obtained, and PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 was negative.

A 54-year-old African American woman with poorly controlled hypertension, a 15 pack-year smoking history, and alpha-thalassemia anemia presented after 3 weeks of progressive blurred vision, fatigue, headache, and orthopnea. She was referred for hypertensive retinopathy evaluation, where her blood pressure measured 220/130 mmHg and she had cotton-wool spots on funduscopic exam. In the emergency department, her systolic pressure reached 230 mmHg. On examination, jugular venous pressure was 14 cm above the sternal angle; heart sounds were distant without pulsus paradoxus; lungs were clear; and there was no peripheral edema. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL (baseline 10 g/dL), creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, C-reactive protein 11 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 110 mm/hr. Chest radiography demonstrated a markedly enlarged cardiac silhouette with mild pulmonary congestion. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large circumferential pericardial effusion (2.24 cm) with early right ventricular diastolic collapse, respirophasic mitral inflow variation, and a dilated inferior vena cava. Contrast-enhanced CT angiography of the chest and cardiac MRI showed no pericardial or pleural thickening, masses, or aortic dissection. She underwent pericardiocentesis yielding 1160 mL of straw-colored fluid. A rheumatologic workup revealed an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:640, positive anti-Smith antibodies, and low complement levels (C3, C4). High-dose intravenous steroids were administered, and a repeat echocardiogram two days later showed reduction of the effusion. Pericardial fluid cytology showed few reactive mesothelial cells and a predominantly lymphocytic infiltrate; bacterial, viral, and fungal studies were negative. Immunohistochemical staining of the fluid was positive for calretinin and weakly positive for CK5/6 and MOC31.

A 5-month-old dark-skinned boy was seen for evaluation of a congenital skin lesion on the left supraclavicular area. At birth, the lesion measured 11 cm × 3.5 cm; at 5 months it measured 10 cm × 2.5 cm. On examination, it was a single, nonpulsatile, well-demarcated, dark brown atrophic plaque with a linear midline depression and an elevated, compressible, soft border that was paler than the central portion. Birth and neonatal history were unremarkable; the patient was healthy and not on medications. The initial differential diagnosis included smooth muscle hamartoma, semiannular lipoatrophy, and, less likely, a rapidly involuting congenital hemangioma (RICH). A small vein (~0.3 mm) was visible to the naked eye within the plaque. To avoid puncturing larger vessels during a planned biopsy, an AccuVein AV400 infrared vein finder was used; it revealed one large vein with an extensive network of small superficial branching vessels localized to the area of the atrophic plaque. A working diagnosis of probable RICH was made.

A 67-year-old woman with a 4-day history of fever and cough was admitted to a local hospital, where SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed by nasopharyngeal PCR. Five days after admission, her respiratory status worsened, prompting intubation and transfer to the ICU. Her comorbidities included diabetes mellitus with dialysis-dependent nephropathy, angina, prior gastric cancer resection, and spinal‐canal stenosis; she was on an antiplatelet agent.  
On arrival: temperature 34 °C; blood pressure 110/65 mmHg; heart rate 102 beats/min; GCS E1VtM1 under deep sedation. Arterial blood gas (on pressure‐control ventilation: PEEP 8 cmH₂O, PiP 25 cmH₂O, FiO₂ 0.5) showed pH 7.309, PaCO₂ 41.5 mmHg, PaO₂ 78.2 mmHg.  
Laboratory studies: WBC 13,900/µL; CRP 13.1 mg/dL; D-dimer 7.25 µg/mL; APTT 170 s; INR 1.35.  
Chest CT: bilateral ground‐glass opacities with lower-lung predominance. Abdominal CT: no overt abnormalities or thromboembolism, but diffuse edema of the intestine, including the transverse colon, and marked sclerotic changes in abdominal vessels.  
She continued dexamethasone (6 mg/day) and commenced continuous renal replacement therapy. On ICU day 3, cefepime was started for ventilator-associated pneumonia. The APTT fell to 51.5 s, and prophylactic-dose unfractionated heparin was initiated to target an APTT of ~60 s.

A 32-year-old man presented with a six-year history of a painless swelling in the left supraclavicular region that had gradually enlarged from the size of an almond to that of a lime. He reported no history of trauma, fever, or systemic illness, and no weakness, numbness, or loss of function in the upper limb. On examination, there was a 4.0-cm diameter, round, firm, non-tender mass in the left supraclavicular area that was mobile in the medio-lateral direction. An ultrasound showed a superficial heterogeneous round cystic mass measuring 47 × 33 mm lateral to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, with well-defined smooth margins and multiple intralesional septa; its lower border lay adjacent to the subclavian artery and its medial border abutted the carotid artery and external jugular vein. The ultrasound was interpreted as a branchial cleft cyst with an atypical location. Fine needle aspiration was performed, and the cystogram findings corroborated this diagnosis. The patient was scheduled for surgical excision of the suspected branchial cleft cyst.

A 28-year-old man was admitted with a 2-day history of intermittent, sharp, central chest pain with diaphoresis. The pain was pleuritic and worsened when he sat forward. He denied recent viral symptoms and had not received a COVID-19 booster. His medical history was significant for ulcerative colitis diagnosed 3 weeks earlier, for which he started mesalazine; his bowel symptoms had improved. He took no other medications and had no allergies. He smoked 3–4 cigarettes daily and denied alcohol or drug use. There was no family history of cardiovascular disease.

On examination he was hemodynamically stable; the only abnormal finding was stage 2 finger clubbing. ECG showed sinus rhythm with benign early repolarization in the anterior leads. Chest radiography was unremarkable. Laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin concentration of 132 g/L (120–170), a low mean corpuscular volume of 75 fL (80–97), and a high-sensitivity troponin T of 275 ng/L (<14) peaking at 632 ng/L on hospital day 2. C-reactive protein was 59 mg/L (<5) rising to 173 mg/L. Serum viral and autoantibody screens were negative.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed a normal left ventricular size, borderline low systolic function (LVEF 50–55%) with dyssynchronous septal motion, and a normal right ventricle without pericardial effusion. Given his atypical pain, young age, and troponin rise, an invasive coronary angiogram was considered but deferred in favor of cardiac magnetic resonance imaging.

On hospital day 3, CMR demonstrated a normal-sized left ventricle with mild systolic dysfunction (LVEF 59%) and hypokinesia of the anterolateral and inferolateral segments. The basal lateral wall was thickened to 14 mm. The right ventricle was small with normal function. There was extensive patchy late gadolinium enhancement in a mid-wall to epicardial distribution, particularly in the basal and mid lateral wall. T2-weighted imaging suggested myocardial edema despite suboptimal image quality. There was no pericardial enhancement or effusion. These findings were consistent with an extensive inflammatory myocardial process.

A 26-year-old woman from Assam, nonsmoker and college student, presented with a 1-month history of dry cough and high-grade intermittent fever. Over the past 15 days she had right-sided, non-radiating chest pain, progressive dyspnea (from mMRC Grade 1 to Grade 3), and an 8-kg weight loss. Initial chest radiography showed an air–fluid level in the right hemithorax. Chest CT revealed a moderate right hydropneumothorax with pleural thickening, right lower‐lobe collapse–consolidation, and no mediastinal lymphadenopathy. 

Right intercostal drainage was placed; pleural fluid was frankly purulent with glucose 20 mg/dL, protein 6.14 g/dL, albumin 2.74 g/dL, LDH 2183 U/L, ADA 119.7 U/L, and a neutrophil‐predominant leukocytosis. Pleural fluid cytology showed an acute inflammatory process with no malignant cells. Empirical four-drug antitubercular therapy was initiated, but the air leak persisted at >100 mL/day and she could not tolerate the medications.

On referral, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable (BP 110/70 mmHg, SpO2 95% on room air). Examination revealed amphoric breath sounds over the right chest and a continuous Grade-4 air leak from the chest tube. Labs showed anemia (Hb 9.6 g/dL) and peripheral eosinophilia (552 cells/mm3); other results, including viral markers, ECG, and echocardiography, were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography identified a probable liver hemangioma; stool microscopy was normal, and amoebic serology was negative.

Because of the persistent air leak and nonexpanding lung, she underwent right‐sided VATS decortication and repair of a bronchopleural fistula. Intraoperative tissue was sent for smear, cultures, and GeneXpert.

clinical_record:
A 1-year-old girl was brought with sudden onset of hematemesis; the vomitus resembled coffee grounds. She was born full-term, had no significant medical or family history, no allergies, and no medication use, including NSAIDs. On arrival she was lethargic; temperature 36.8 °C, heart rate 160 bpm, respiratory rate 24 bpm, blood pressure 83/35 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 100% on 2 L nasal oxygen. Physical examination showed pallor but was otherwise unremarkable. A nasogastric tube aspirated a small amount of blood. Laboratory tests revealed WBC 9,500/μL; hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL; platelets 220×10^3/μL; CRP 0.55 mg/dL; normal liver function tests; prothrombin time 13.2 s (INR 1.01); aPTT 31.7 s; normal factor XIII and plasma gastrin levels; ESR 2 mm/h. Serologies for cytomegalovirus-IgM, EBV-VCA-IgM, and H. pylori-IgG were negative, and stool antigen testing excluded H. pylori. Blood cultures and stool parasite testing were negative. Abdominal radiography and ultrasonography were normal, and contrast-enhanced CT showed no active bleeding. She received two units of packed red blood cells and famotidine, yet her hemoglobin remained low. Thus, on hospital day 2, early upper endoscopy was planned to identify the bleeding source.

A man in his 40s with a medical history of factor VII deficiency hemophilia presented with acute hypoxic respiratory failure. Following admission, he was intubated with prone positioning, and treatment was initiated. He was also found to have Staphylococcus hemolyticus bacteremia. Three days after admission, the patient developed erythema and edematous necrotic plaques of the bilateral ears. No devices had been used on the ears. The necrosis progressed during the following days, primarily involving the earlobe of the right ear and a large portion of the helix of the left ear.

Erythematous plaque (2 cm) with overlying eschar on the right earlobe. Multiple erythematous edematous erosions with eschar and crust on the helical rim of the left ear.
